St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre. It was a multi-day spree of Catholic violence against French Protestant Huguenots beginning August 24, 1572, in Paris and spreading to provincial towns across France. The trigger was a failed assassination attempt on Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, a Huguenot leader. This sparked hysteria among Catholic mobs and the royal court that conspirators were plotting to seize power. Organized ostensibly under the authority of King Charles IX and enabled by his mother Catherine de Medici, thousands of Huguenots were slaughtered in their homes, streets, and churches. The massacre became a defining atrocity of the French Wars of Religion and shattered the fragile peace that had held since 1570.

An assassination attempt on Gaspard de Coligny on August 22 failed, though the Admiral was wounded but survived. Huguenot princes demanded the arrest and trial of the would-be assassins, but Catherine de Medici and the Catholic faction saw this as a threat to royal authority. King Charles IX and the court panicked, fearing a Huguenot insurrection, and ordered the massacre to preempt it.

The killing began in the early morning of August 24, the feast day of St. Bartholomew, when Catholic mobs rampaged through Paris for three days. An estimated 2,000 to 3,000 Huguenots were killed in Paris alone, with some estimates placing the total death toll across France at 10,000 or more. Entire families were murdered in their beds, churches where Huguenots sought refuge were set alight, and bodies were mutilated and dragged through streets.

Gaspard de Coligny was dragged from his sickbed and murdered, his body desecrated and hanged from a gibbet. Other prominent Huguenot leaders were killed, their wives and children perishing alongside them. The violence was indiscriminate, with common folk and nobility alike targeted based on religion.

The massacre turned the Huguenots from a potentially loyal minority into an entrenched opposition force and hardened religious divisions in France. It vindicated Huguenot fears of Catholic persecution, and subsequent peace treaties were more fragile. Henry of Navarre, a Huguenot prince, survived by abjuring his faith temporarily, but he later returned to Protestantism and eventually granted the Edict of Nantes in 1598. The massacre was instantly mythologized, with Catholics calling it a justified defense of the Crown and Protestants calling it premeditated genocide. These competing narratives became foundational to how each side understood the conflict, delaying by two decades any durable settlement and costing the nation untold wealth and stability.
